claim: Cytokines activate signaling via assembly of cell surface receptors.
source: Cytokines activate signaling via assembly of cell surface receptors, but it is unclear whether modulation of cytokine-receptor binding parameters can modify biological outcomes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of cytokine biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: It is unclear whether modulation of cytokine-receptor binding parameters can modify biological outcomes.
source: Cytokines activate signaling via assembly of cell surface receptors, but it is unclear whether modulation of cytokine-receptor binding parameters can modify biological outcomes.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Engineered IL-6 variants showed a range of signaling amplitudes.
source: Engineered IL-6 variants showed a range of signaling amplitudes and induced biased signaling, with changes in receptor binding dwell-times affecting more profoundly STAT1 than STAT3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential STAT phosphorylation levels.

claim: Engineered IL-6 variants induced biased signaling.
source: Engineered IL-6 variants showed a range of signaling amplitudes and induced biased signaling, with changes in receptor binding dwell-times affecting more profoundly STAT1 than STAT3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential STAT1 and STAT3 activation patterns.

claim: Changes in receptor binding dwell-times affect STAT1 phosphorylation more profoundly than STAT3 phosphorylation.
source: Engineered IL-6 variants showed a range of signaling amplitudes and induced biased signaling, with changes in receptor binding dwell-times affecting more profoundly STAT1 than STAT3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of STAT1 and STAT3 phosphorylation levels in response to different IL-6 variants.

claim: Differential signaling arises from defective translocation of ligand-gp130 complexes to the endosomal compartment.
source: We show that this differential signaling arises from defective translocation of ligand-gp130 complexes to the endosomal compartment and competitive STAT1/STAT3 binding to phospho-tyrosines in gp130, and results in unique patterns of STAT3 binding to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and flow cytometry data showing differential internalization of IL-6 variants.

claim: Differential signaling arises from competitive STAT1/STAT3 binding to phospho-tyrosines in gp130.
source: We show that this differential signaling arises from defective translocation of ligand-gp130 complexes to the endosomal compartment and competitive STAT1/STAT3 binding to phospho-tyrosines in gp130, and results in unique patterns of STAT3 binding to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with gp130 mutants and STAT3 knockdown/overexpression studies.

claim: Biased signaling results in unique patterns of STAT3 binding to chromatin.
source: We show that this differential signaling arises from defective translocation of ligand-gp130 complexes to the endosomal compartment and competitive STAT1/STAT3 binding to phospho-tyrosines in gp130, and results in unique patterns of STAT3 binding to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing differential STAT3 binding patterns.

claim: Biased signaling leads to a graded gene expression response.
source: This leads to a graded gene expression response and differences in ex vivo differentiation of Th17, Th1 and Treg cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: Biased signaling leads to differences in ex vivo differentiation of Th17, Th1 and Treg cells.
source: This leads to a graded gene expression response and differences in ex vivo differentiation of Th17, Th1 and Treg cells.
evidence: This is supported by T cell differentiation assays showing differential effects on Th17, Th1, and Treg populations.

claim: Manipulation of signaling thresholds is a useful strategy to decouple cytokine functional pleiotropy.
source: These results provide a molecular understanding of signaling biased by cytokine receptors, and demonstrate that manipulation of signaling thresholds is a useful strategy to decouple cytokine functional pleiotropy.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential biological activities of IL-6 variants.

claim: Cytokines modulate the immune response by activating a common JAK/STAT signaling pathway upon cell surface receptor dimerization/oligomerization.
source: Cytokines modulate the immune response by activating a common JAK/STAT signaling pathway upon cell surface receptor dimerization/oligomerization (Gorby et al., 2018; Stroud and Wells, 2004; Wang et al., 2009; Wells et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this mechanism.

claim: There are four JAKs and seven STATs in the cytokine signaling system.
source: A conundrum in the field pertains to how biological specificity is achieved in the cytokine system by using such reduced number of signaling intermediaries, that is four JAKs and seven STATs (Murray, 2007; Schindler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: IL-6 and IL-10 activate the same STATs in CD4 T cells.
source: Indeed, there are numerous examples in the literature where cytokines activating the same STATs in CD4 T cells, for example IL-6 and IL-10 (Grotzinger et al., 1997; Walter, 2004), produce opposite responses, that is pro-inflammatory vs anti-inflammatory responses respectively (Hunter and Jones, 2015; Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IL-6 produces pro-inflammatory responses.
source: Indeed, there are numerous examples in the literature where cytokines activating the same STATs in CD4 T cells, for example IL-6 and IL-10 (Grotzinger et al., 1997; Walter, 2004), produce opposite responses, that is pro-inflammatory vs anti-inflammatory responses respectively (Hunter and Jones, 2015; Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IL-10 produces anti-inflammatory responses.
source: Indeed, there are numerous examples in the literature where cytokines activating the same STATs in CD4 T cells, for example IL-6 and IL-10 (Grotzinger et al., 1997; Walter, 2004), produce opposite responses, that is pro-inflammatory vs anti-inflammatory responses respectively (Hunter and Jones, 2015; Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cytokine signaling is not an 'all or none' phenomenon and can be modulated by alterations of cytokine-receptor binding properties.
source: In recent years, a number of studies in multiple cytokine systems have shown that cytokine signaling is not an 'all or none' phenomenon and can be modulated by alterations of cytokine-receptor binding properties (Spangler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Changes in cytokine-receptor binding kinetics and strength play a crucial role in defining type I and type III interferons biological potencies.
source: Changes in cytokine-receptor binding kinetics and strength were shown to play a crucial role in defining type I and type III interferons biological potencies (Mendoza et al., 2017; Pestka, 2007; Piehler et al., 2012; Subramaniam et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A mutation in erythropoietin (Epo) found in humans reduces its binding affinity for its receptor (EpoR).
source: A mutation in erythropoietin (Epo) found in humans, which reduces its binding affinity for its receptor (EpoR), was shown to bias signaling output by EpoR and caused severe anemia in human patients (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A mutation in erythropoietin that reduces its binding affinity for EpoR biases signaling output by EpoR.
source: A mutation in erythropoietin (Epo) found in humans, which reduces its binding affinity for its receptor (EpoR), was shown to bias signaling output by EpoR and caused severe anemia in human patients (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A mutation in erythropoietin that reduces its binding affinity for EpoR caused severe anemia in human patients.
source: A mutation in erythropoietin (Epo) found in humans, which reduces its binding affinity for its receptor (EpoR), was shown to bias signaling output by EpoR and caused severe anemia in human patients (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Biased EpoR signaling was achieved using surrogate Epo ligands that altered the receptor binding topology.
source: Biased EpoR signaling was also achieved using surrogate Epo ligands that altered the receptor binding topology (Moraga et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Viruses encode cytokine-like proteins that bind cytokine receptors with altered binding properties.
source: Viruses often encode for cytokine-like proteins that bind cytokine receptors with altered binding properties, providing them with means to fine-tune the immune response to their own advantage (Boulanger et al., 2004; Walter, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Viral cytokine-like proteins provide viruses with means to fine-tune the immune response to their own advantage.
source: Viruses often encode for cytokine-like proteins that bind cytokine receptors with altered binding properties, providing them with means to fine-tune the immune response to their own advantage (Boulanger et al., 2004; Walter, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents an inference about viral strategy.

claim: A model providing molecular bases for signaling biased by cytokine receptor is missing.
source: All these examples strongly argue in favour of cytokine-receptor binding parameters contributing to regulate signaling, however a model providing molecular bases for signaling biased by cytokine receptor is missing.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Biased signaling is not a unique feature of the cytokine family.
source: Biased signaling is not a unique feature of the cytokine family.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cell signaling.

claim: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the classical system where biased signaling was first described.
source: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which contain seven-transmembrane domains, are the classical system where biased signaling was first described (Hilger et al., 2018; Wootten et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: GPCRs contain seven-transmembrane domains.
source: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which contain seven-transmembrane domains, are the classical system where biased signaling was first described (Hilger et al., 2018; Wootten et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR structure.

claim: In GPCRs, different ligands binding a common receptor can trigger differential signaling programs by instructing specific allosteric changes in the transmembrane α-helices of the receptor.
source: In this system, different ligands binding a common receptor can trigger differential signaling programs by instructing specific allosteric changes in the transmembrane α-helices of the receptor (Hilger et al., 2018; Wootten et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The GPCR mechanism of biased signaling is more difficult to imagine for cytokine receptors where the transmembrane (TM) region contributes less significantly to signaling.
source: However, this mechanism is more difficult to imagine for cytokine receptors where the transmembrane (TM) region contributes less significantly to signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional differences between GPCRs and cytokine receptors.

claim: Cytokine receptor chimeras where their TM has been swapped by that of other receptors still trigger signaling.
source: Cytokine receptor chimeras where their TM has been swapped by that of other receptors still trigger signaling (Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Upon ligand stimulation cytokine-receptor complexes traffic to intracellular compartments, where they are often degraded.
source: A common feature to all cytokine systems is that upon ligand stimulation cytokine-receptor complexes traffic to intracellular compartments, where they are often degraded, contributing to switching off the response (Becker et al., 2010; Bulut et al., 2011; Claudinon et al., 2007; German et al., 2011; Keeler et al., 2007; Shah et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Degradation of cytokine-receptor complexes in intracellular compartments contributes to switching off the response.
source: A common feature to all cytokine systems is that upon ligand stimulation cytokine-receptor complexes traffic to intracellular compartments, where they are often degraded, contributing to switching off the response (Becker et al., 2010; Bulut et al., 2011; Claudinon et al., 2007; German et al., 2011; Keeler et al., 2007; Shah et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A complex positive regulatory role of endocytosis in cytokine signaling has emerged.
source: However, a complex positive regulatory role of endocytosis in cytokine signaling has emerged (Becker et al., 2010; Cendrowski et al., 2016; Fallon and Lauffenburger, 2000; Marchetti et al., 2006; Sarkar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The endosomal compartment stabilizes cytokine receptor dimers by enhancing local receptor concentrations.
source: Several studies recently suggested a novel role for the endosomal compartment in stabilizing cytokine receptor dimers by enhancing local receptor concentrations (Gandhi et al., 2014; Moraga et al., 2015a), thus contributing to signaling fitness even at low complex stabilities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endosomal stabilization of cytokine receptor dimers contributes to signaling fitness even at low complex stabilities.
source: Several studies recently suggested a novel role for the endosomal compartment in stabilizing cytokine receptor dimers by enhancing local receptor concentrations (Gandhi et al., 2014; Moraga et al., 2015a), thus contributing to signaling fitness even at low complex stabilities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents an inference about the functional consequence.

claim: Mutations on cytokine receptors that alter their intracellular traffic can result in activation of novel or deregulated signaling programs causing disease.
source: In agreement with this model, mutations on cytokine receptors that alter their intracellular traffic can result in activation of novel or deregulated signaling programs causing disease (Reddy et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activated JAK/STAT proteins have been described in endosomes after interferon stimulation.
source: Furthermore, activated JAK/STAT proteins have been described in endosomes after interferon stimulation, suggesting that signaling continues upon receptor internalization (Payelle-Brogard and Pellegrini, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Signaling continues upon receptor internalization.
source: Furthermore, activated JAK/STAT proteins have been described in endosomes after interferon stimulation, suggesting that signaling continues upon receptor internalization (Payelle-Brogard and Pellegrini, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of activated JAK/STAT proteins in endosomes.

claim: IL-6 is a highly pleiotropic cytokine.
source: IL-6 is a highly pleiotropic cytokine, which critically contributes to mounting the inflammatory response (Grotzinger et al., 1997; Hunter and Jones, 2015; Naka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: IL-6 critically contributes to mounting the inflammatory response.
source: IL-6 is a highly pleiotropic cytokine, which critically contributes to mounting the inflammatory response (Grotzinger et al., 1997; Hunter and Jones, 2015; Naka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IL-6 stimulation drives differentiation of Th17 cells.
source: IL-6 stimulation drives differentiation of Th17 cells (Jones et al., 2010; Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010; Louten et al., 2009), and inhibits the differentiation of Th1 (Diehl and Rincón, 2002) and T regulatory (reg) cells (Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010; Korn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IL-6 inhibits the differentiation of Th1 cells.
source: IL-6 stimulation drives differentiation of Th17 cells (Jones et al., 2010; Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010; Louten et al., 2009), and inhibits the differentiation of Th1 (Diehl and Rincón, 2002) and T regulatory (reg) cells (Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010; Korn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IL-6 inhibits the differentiation of T regulatory cells.
source: IL-6 stimulation drives differentiation of Th17 cells (Jones et al., 2010; Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010; Louten et al., 2009), and inhibits the differentiation of Th1 (Diehl and Rincón, 2002) and T regulatory (reg) cells (Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010; Korn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deregulation of IL-6 levels and activities is often found in human diseases.
source: Deregulation of IL-6 levels and activities is often found in human diseases, making IL-6 a very attractive therapeutic target (Hunter and Jones, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: IL-6 is a very attractive therapeutic target.
source: Deregulation of IL-6 levels and activities is often found in human diseases, making IL-6 a very attractive therapeutic target (Hunter and Jones, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of IL-6 in disease, supported by citation.

claim: IL-6 exerts its immuno-modulatory activities by engaging a hexameric complex comprised of two molecules of IL-6Rα, two molecules of gp130 and two molecules of IL-6.
source: IL-6 exerts its immuno-modulatory activities by engaging a hexameric complex comprised of two molecules of IL-6Rα, two molecules of gp130 and two molecules of IL-6, leading to the downstream activation of STAT1 and STAT3 transcription factors (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge about IL-6 signaling mechanism.

claim: IL-6 hexameric complex formation leads to the downstream activation of STAT1 and STAT3 transcription factors.
source: IL-6 exerts its immuno-modulatory activities by engaging a hexameric complex comprised of two molecules of IL-6Rα, two molecules of gp130 and two molecules of IL-6, leading to the downstream activation of STAT1 and STAT3 transcription factors (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A series of IL-6 variants binding gp130 with different affinities were isolated, ranging from wild-type binding affinity to more than 2000-fold enhanced binding.
source: Using the yeast-surface display engineering platform, we isolated a series of IL-6 variants binding gp130 with different affinities, ranging from wild-type binding affinity to more than 2000-fold enhanced binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from yeast surface display and SPR studies.

claim: Reduction in cytokine-receptor complex stability resulted in differential cytokine-receptor complex dynamics.
source: Quantitative signaling and imaging studies revealed that reduction in cytokine-receptor complex stability resulted in differential cytokine-receptor complex dynamics, which ultimately led to activation of biased signaling programs.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy and confocal imaging data.

claim: Differential cytokine-receptor complex dynamics led to activation of biased signaling programs.
source: Quantitative signaling and imaging studies revealed that reduction in cytokine-receptor complex stability resulted in differential cytokine-receptor complex dynamics, which ultimately led to activation of biased signaling programs.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data showing differential STAT activation.

claim: Low affinity IL-6 variants failed to translocate to intracellular compartments.
source: Low affinity IL-6 variants failed to translocate to intracellular compartments and induce gp130 degradation, triggering STAT3 biased responses.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy and flow cytometry data showing reduced internalization.

claim: Low affinity IL-6 variants failed to induce gp130 degradation.
source: Low affinity IL-6 variants failed to translocate to intracellular compartments and induce gp130 degradation, triggering STAT3 biased responses.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing gp130 levels over time.

claim: Low affinity IL-6 variants trigger STAT3 biased responses.
source: Low affinity IL-6 variants failed to translocate to intracellular compartments and induce gp130 degradation, triggering STAT3 biased responses.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data showing differential STAT3/STAT1 activation ratios.

claim: Inhibition of gp130 intracellular translocation by chemical blockage of clathrin-mediated trafficking reduced STAT1 activation levels without affecting STAT3 activation.
source: Indeed, inhibition of gp130 intracellular translocation by chemical or genetic blockage of clathrin-mediated trafficking, reduced STAT1 activation levels, without affecting STAT3 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Pitstop inhibitor showing differential effects on STAT1 and STAT3.

claim: Inhibition of gp130 intracellular translocation by genetic blockage of clathrin-mediated trafficking reduced STAT1 activation levels without affecting STAT3 activation.
source: Indeed, inhibition of gp130 intracellular translocation by chemical or genetic blockage of clathrin-mediated trafficking, reduced STAT1 activation levels, without affecting STAT3 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using clathrin siRNA showing differential effects on STAT1 and STAT3.

claim: STAT1 requires a higher number of phospho-Tyr available in gp130 to reach maximal activation.
source: Through a series of molecular and cellular assays we demonstrated that STAT1 requires a higher number of phospho-Tyr available in gp130 to reach maximal activation, explaining its enhanced sensitivity to changes in cytokine-receptor dwell-times.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with gp130 chimeras and Tyr-to-Phe mutants.

claim: STAT1's requirement for a higher number of phospho-Tyr explains its enhanced sensitivity to changes in cytokine-receptor dwell-times.
source: Through a series of molecular and cellular assays we demonstrated that STAT1 requires a higher number of phospho-Tyr available in gp130 to reach maximal activation, explaining its enhanced sensitivity to changes in cytokine-receptor dwell-times.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing STAT1's requirement for more phospho-Tyr sites.

claim: The biased signaling programs engaged by the IL-6 variants did not have a linear effect on STAT3 transcriptional activities.
source: The biased signaling programs engaged by the IL-6 variants did not have a linear effect on STAT3 transcriptional activities.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing non-linear gene expression responses.

claim: Reduced STAT3 activation levels by the low affinity IL-6 variants resulted in graded STAT3 binding to chromatin.
source: Reduced STAT3 activation levels by the low affinity IL-6 variants resulted in graded STAT3 binding to chromatin and gene expression, with some genes exhibiting a high degree of sensitivity to STAT3 activation levels, and other genes being equally induced by all three IL-6 variants.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing differential STAT3 binding intensities.

claim: Reduced STAT3 activation levels by the low affinity IL-6 variants resulted in graded gene expression.
source: Reduced STAT3 activation levels by the low affinity IL-6 variants resulted in graded STAT3 binding to chromatin and gene expression, with some genes exhibiting a high degree of sensitivity to STAT3 activation levels, and other genes being equally induced by all three IL-6 variants.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: Some genes exhibit a high degree of sensitivity to STAT3 activation levels.
source: Reduced STAT3 activation levels by the low affinity IL-6 variants resulted in graded STAT3 binding to chromatin and gene expression, with some genes exhibiting a high degree of sensitivity to STAT3 activation levels, and other genes being equally induced by all three IL-6 variants.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression responses to IL-6 variants.

claim: Some genes are equally induced by all three IL-6 variants.
source: Reduced STAT3 activation levels by the low affinity IL-6 variants resulted in graded STAT3 binding to chromatin and gene expression, with some genes exhibiting a high degree of sensitivity to STAT3 activation levels, and other genes being equally induced by all three IL-6 variants.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing similar gene expression levels across IL-6 variants for certain genes.

claim: Th17 differentiation was induced by all three IL-6 variants.
source: Moreover, IL-6 immuno-modulatory activities exhibited different sensitivity thresholds to changes on STAT activation levels, with Th17 differentiation being induced by all three variants, and inhibition of Treg and Th1 differentiation only robustly promoted by the high affinity variant.
evidence: This is supported by T cell differentiation assays.

claim: Inhibition of Treg differentiation was only robustly promoted by the high affinity IL-6 variant.
source: Moreover, IL-6 immuno-modulatory activities exhibited different sensitivity thresholds to changes on STAT activation levels, with Th17 differentiation being induced by all three variants, and inhibition of Treg and Th1 differentiation only robustly promoted by the high affinity variant.
evidence: This is supported by T cell differentiation assays.

claim: Inhibition of Th1 differentiation was only robustly promoted by the high affinity IL-6 variant.
source: Moreover, IL-6 immuno-modulatory activities exhibited different sensitivity thresholds to changes on STAT activation levels, with Th17 differentiation being induced by all three variants, and inhibition of Treg and Th1 differentiation only robustly promoted by the high affinity variant.
evidence: This is supported by T cell differentiation assays.

claim: IL-6 triggers signaling by assembling a hexameric complex probably in a three steps process.
source: IL-6 triggers signaling by assembling a hexameric complex probably in a three steps process (Figure 1a): IL-6 first binds to the IL-6Rα receptor subunit with nanomolar affinity via its site-1 binding interface.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: IL-6 first binds to the IL-6Rα receptor subunit with nanomolar affinity via its site-1 binding interface.
source: IL-6 first binds to the IL-6Rα receptor subunit with nanomolar affinity via its site-1 binding interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-6 signaling mechanism.

claim: The IL-6/IL-6Rα complex recruits one molecule of gp130 via IL-6 site-2 binding interface to form a hetero-trimeric complex.
source: In the second step, the IL-6/IL-6Rα complex recruits one molecule of gp130 via IL-6 site-2 binding interface to form a hetero-trimeric complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-6 signaling mechanism.

claim: Two hetero-trimeric complexes dimerize via the IL-6 site-3 binding sites to form a signalling-active hexameric complex.
source: Finally, two of these hetero-trimeric complexes dimerize via the IL-6 site-3 binding sites to form a signalling-active hexameric complex (Figure 1a, top panel) (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: IL-6Rα contributes to stabilize site-2 and site-3 interaction of IL-6 by directly interacting with gp130.
source: Importantly, IL-6Rα further contributes to stabilize site-2 and site-3 interaction of IL-6 by directly interacting with gp130 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a showing structural interactions.

claim: In an inflammatory environment, IL-6Rα is shed from the plasma membrane via proteases of the ADAM family.
source: In an inflammatory environment, IL-6Rα is shed from the plasma membrane via proteases of the ADAM family, and binds IL-6 with high affinity to form a soluble stable complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-6 trans-signaling.

claim: Soluble IL-6Rα binds IL-6 with high affinity to form a soluble stable complex.
source: In an inflammatory environment, IL-6Rα is shed from the plasma membrane via proteases of the ADAM family, and binds IL-6 with high affinity to form a soluble stable complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-6 trans-signaling.

claim: The soluble IL-6/IL-6Rα complex triggers potent signaling by recruiting two molecules of gp130 via site-2 and site-3 IL-6 binding interfaces.
source: This complex triggers potent signaling by recruiting two molecules of gp130 via site-2 and site-3 IL-6 binding interfaces therefore contributing to enhance the inflammatory response (Figure 1a, middle panel) (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The soluble IL-6/IL-6Rα complex contributes to enhance the inflammatory response.
source: This complex triggers potent signaling by recruiting two molecules of gp130 via site-2 and site-3 IL-6 binding interfaces therefore contributing to enhance the inflammatory response (Figure 1a, middle panel) (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the potent signaling triggered by the complex, supported by citation.

claim: The inflammatory complex can be mimicked by a linker-connected single-chain variant of soluble IL-6Rα and IL-6, called hyper-IL-6 (HyIL-6).
source: This inflammatory complex can be mimicked by a linker-connected single-chain variant of soluble IL-6Rα and IL-6, called hyper-IL-6 (HyIL-6) (Fischer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: IL-6 interacts with gp130 on two sites, named site-2 and site-3.
source: As described above, IL-6 interacts with gp130 on two sites, named site-2, which uses helixes A and C on IL-6, and site-3 which uses part of the AB-loop and helix D (Figure 1b) (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Site-2 uses helixes A and C on IL-6.
source: As described above, IL-6 interacts with gp130 on two sites, named site-2, which uses helixes A and C on IL-6, and site-3 which uses part of the AB-loop and helix D (Figure 1b) (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Site-3 uses part of the AB-loop and helix D on IL-6.
source: As described above, IL-6 interacts with gp130 on two sites, named site-2, which uses helixes A and C on IL-6, and site-3 which uses part of the AB-loop and helix D (Figure 1b) (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The site-2 binding interface is the main driver of gp130-IL6 interaction in the absence of IL-6Rα.
source: We focused on the site-2 binding interface because this interface seems to be the main driver of gp130-IL6 interaction in the absence of IL-6Rα.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional knowledge of IL-6 signaling.

claim: 14 amino acids on IL-6 forming the site-2 binding interface were randomized using a 'NDT' degenerate codon.
source: Using the existing crystal structure of the IL-6 hexameric complex, we identified 14 amino acids on IL-6 forming the site-2 binding interface, which we randomized using a 'NDT' degenerate codon encoding amino acids: G,V,L,I,C,S,R,H,D,N,F,Y (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for library generation.

claim: The IL-6 library contained more than 3 × 10^8 unique variants.
source: The resulting library contained more than 3 × 108 unique variants.
evidence: This is a measurement of library diversity.

claim: The library was selected for gp130 binders through five rounds of selection in which the gp130 concentration was gradually decreased from 1 μM to 1 nM.
source: The library was selected for gp130 binders through five rounds of selection in which the gp130 concentration was gradually decreased from 1 μM to 1 nM (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This describes the experimental selection strategy, illustrated in Figure 1c-e.

claim: Nine clones were selected based on their on-yeast binding titrations.
source: Nine clones were selected based on their on-yeast binding titrations and their sequences were obtained (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental selection process.

claim: IL-6 variants exhibiting a wide range of binding affinities for gp130 were isolated, ranging from wild type (wt) affinity (A1) to 200-fold better binding (F3).
source: From this initial library, IL-6 variants exhibiting a wide range of binding affinities for gp130 were isolated, ranging from wild type (wt) affinity (A1) to 200-fold better binding (F3) (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by on-yeast binding titration data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Three new variants (Mut1, Mut3 and Mut7) bound gp130 with an apparent on-yeast binding KD of 2 nM.
source: After five additional rounds of selection we isolated three new variants (Mut1, Mut3 and Mut7) that bound gp130 with an apparent on-yeast binding KD of 2 nM (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by on-yeast binding titration data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: SPR studies confirm the same trend observed in the on-yeast binding titration experiments, with KD values ranging from 648 nM (A1) to 6.2 nM (C7) and 379 pM (Mut3).
source: These studies confirm the same trend observed in the on-yeast binding titration experiments, with values ranging from 648 nM (A1) to 6.2 nM (C7) and 379 pM (Mut3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-d).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: The engineered IL-6 variants still exhibit wt binding affinity for gp130 via their site-3 interfaces.
source: It is important to emphasize that our engineered IL-6 variants still exhibit wt binding affinity for gp130 via their site-3 interfaces.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that only site-2 was engineered.

claim: The overall half-life of the tetrameric surface complex formed by the IL-6 variants is defined by their combined site-2/site-3 binding interaction.
source: Thus, although they bind gp130 in the absence of IL-6Rα, the overall half-life of the tetrameric surface complex formed by these variants is defined by their combined site-2/site-3 binding interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding mechanism of IL-6 variants.

claim: HyIL-6 forms an even longer-lived complex than any of the engineered IL-6 variants.

claim: Induction of IRF1 expression was more sensitive to changes on gp130 binding affinity than ICAM1 expression.

claim: Strong gp130 dimerization was found for HyIL-6 and Mut3 after cytokine stimulation.

claim: Decreased lateral diffusion mobility can be ascribed to increased friction of dimeric receptors within the membrane.
source: In line with the dimerization, we observed a considerable decrease in lateral diffusion mobility, which can be ascribed to increased friction of dimeric receptors within the membrane (Moraga et al., 2015b; Wilmes et al., 2015) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b-c).
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mut3, C7 and A1 variants led to a poor but detectable transient internalization which correlated with their binding affinity.
source: Mut3, C7 and A1 variants led to a poor but detectable transient internalization which correlated with their binding affinity.

claim: Mut3 induced significantly lower gp130 degradation than HyIL-6.

claim: C7, A1 and IL-6 treatment led to some stabilization of gp130 in the cell surface.

claim: Activation of signaling pathways leading to receptor degradation can be decoupled from STAT1/3 activation by modulating cytokine-receptor complex half-life.

claim: Mut3 activates STAT1 and STAT3 to the same extent as HyIL-6 but induced substantially lower degradation of gp130.
source: Indeed, while Mut3 activates STAT1 and STAT3 to the same extent as HyIL-6, it induced substantially lower degradation of gp130 (Figure 4a–b).

claim: Internalization of HyIL-6 was strongly inhibited by Pitstop treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 4c, internalization of HyIL-6 was strongly inhibited by Pitstop treatment, confirming the ability of this inhibitor to block gp130 internalization.

claim: STAT3 phosphorylation levels induced by the three IL-6 variants did not change when gp130 internalization was blocked.
source: As shown in Figure 4d, the STAT3 phosphorylation levels induced by the three IL-6 variants did not change when gp130 internalization was blocked.

claim: STAT1 activation by Mut3 was not affected by blocking gp130 internalization.
source: STAT1 activation by Mut3 was not affected and A1 failed to activate STAT1 as shown in previous experiments (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data with Pitstop treatment shown in Figure 4c.

claim: STAT1 phosphorylation levels induced by the C7 variant were significantly downregulated in the presence of Pitstop.
source: STAT1 phosphorylation levels induced by the C7 variant on the other hand were significantly downregulated in the presence of Pitstop (Figure 4c), which ultimately led to a more pronounced STAT3/STAT1 activation ratio by this variant (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data with Pitstop treatment shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Blocking gp130 internalization led to a more pronounced STAT3/STAT1 activation ratio by the C7 variant.
source: STAT1 phosphorylation levels induced by the C7 variant on the other hand were significantly downregulated in the presence of Pitstop (Figure 4c), which ultimately led to a more pronounced STAT3/STAT1 activation ratio by this variant (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Pitstop on STAT1 vs STAT3, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Clathrin silencing did not affect STAT3 activation.

claim: Clathrin silencing reduced activation of STAT1 by Mut3 and C7 variants.

evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data with clathrin siRNA shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Translocation of gp130 complexes to intracellular compartments is an important requisite for STAT1 activation by short-lived IL-6-gp130 complexes.
source: Overall, these data indicate that translocation of gp130 complexes to intracellular compartments is an important requisite for STAT1, but not STAT3 activation by short-lived IL-6-gp130 complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Pitstop and clathrin siRNA experiments.

claim: Translocation of gp130 complexes to intracellular compartments is not an important requisite for STAT3 activation by short-lived IL-6-gp130 complexes.
source: Overall, these data indicate that translocation of gp130 complexes to intracellular compartments is an important requisite for STAT1, but not STAT3 activation by short-lived IL-6-gp130 complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Pitstop and clathrin siRNA experiments.

claim: STAT3 binds with higher affinity to phospho-Tyr on gp130 than STAT1.
source: Previous work showed that STAT3, via its SH2 domain, binds with higher affinity to phospho-Tyr on gp130 than STAT1 (Wiederkehr-Adam et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Competitive binding of STAT1 and STAT3 for phospho-Tyr on gp130 would result in differential levels of activation of these two transcription factors in the context of short-lived IL-6/gp130 complexes.
source: We thus postulated that competitive binding of STAT1 and STAT3 for phospho-Tyr on gp130 would result in differential levels of activation of these two transcription factors in the context of short-lived IL-6/gp130 complexes.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on known binding affinities.

claim: IL-27 triggers signaling by dimerizing IL-27Rα and gp130 receptor subunits.
source: IL-27 triggers signaling by dimerizing IL-27Rα and gp130 receptor subunits (Stumhofer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The three RPE1 clones expressing different chimera receptors were homogenous based on their comparable responsiveness to HyIL-6.

As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, HyIL-6 induced comparable levels of STAT1 and STAT3 activation in the three clones, strongly arguing that the endogenous gp130, JAK1, STAT1 and STAT3 levels in the three clones were identical.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The three RPE1 clones produced very similar STAT3 activation levels in response to IL-27.
source: In response to IL-27, the three clones produced very similar STAT3 activation levels, suggesting that STAT3 activation is very efficient and only requires a minimal set of phospho-Tyr available to reach its activation peak (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: STAT3 activation is very efficient and only requires a minimal set of phospho-Tyr available to reach its activation peak.
source: In response to IL-27, the three clones produced very similar STAT3 activation levels, suggesting that STAT3 activation is very efficient and only requires a minimal set of phospho-Tyr available to reach its activation peak (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that STAT3 activation is similar across chimeras with different numbers of phospho-Tyr sites.

claim: STAT1 activation levels dropped by more than fifty percent in the gp130 ΔY clone.
source: However, STAT1 activation levels dropped by more than fifty percent in the gp130 ΔY clone (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), demonstrating that STAT1 activation by gp130 requires a higher number of phospho-Tyr available.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: STAT1 activation by gp130 requires a higher number of phospho-Tyr available.
source: However, STAT1 activation levels dropped by more than fifty percent in the gp130 ΔY clone (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), demonstrating that STAT1 activation by gp130 requires a higher number of phospho-Tyr available.

claim: Single Tyr mutations did not decrease the STAT1/STAT3 activation levels induced by HyIL-6.

evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data with gp130 Tyr mutants.

claim: Mutation of Tyr 815/905/915 produced a 50% decrease on the STAT1 phosphorylation levels induced by HyIL-6 stimulation.

claim: STAT3 silencing did not change the STAT1 activation levels induced by HyIL-6 and Mut3.

claim: There is competition between STAT1 and STAT3 for Tyr in gp130.
